1:
How fair the question was gets three gradations. Clarke allows some colour of justice, on the ground that Stephen was permitted to defend himself at all, and paraphrases what was being asked: hast thou predicted the destruction of the temple, hast thou said that Jesus of Nazareth shall change our customs? Henry allows a show of fairness and no more, the high priest speaking as president of the court but with an air of haughtiness, and having prejudged the case, since if the words were spoken nothing offered in explanation would be heard. Calvin grants a colour of equity and then withdraws it: the question is not what cause Stephen had to teach so, nor is he admitted to a defence of the right of the matter, but only asked whether he uttered the words, whatever they were — and Calvin turns this at once against the tribunals of his own day, which do not ask what the doctrine is or whether it can be proved from Scripture, but only whether a man has dared to mutter against their superstitions, so that once convicted he may be burnt. Ellicott notes that the question is analogous to the one put to Christ, and Robertson matches it to a modern arraignment, do you plead guilty or not guilty.

Why the answer takes the form it does is the substantial question, and four answer it differently. Robertson starts from the charges: two were laid, speaking against the temple and changing the customs Moses delivered, and neither could be met with a yes or a no, since there was an element of truth in each and a large amount of error mixed with it — so Stephen explains his real position by the historical method, the same method Paul afterwards used at Pisidian Antioch. Barnes makes it a matter of what the defence proves and what it can get a hearing for: rehearsing the history avows a belief in the divine origin of the Jewish religion and so repels the charge indirectly, and it is the one way calculated to hold that audience, since an abstract defence would have been stopped by cavil or clamour while the history of their own nation was a subject they would always hear. Calvin concedes the objection before answering it: at first blush the answer looks absurd and foolish, beginning at the very beginning and running to a long narration with hardly any mention of the matter in hand, and there can be no greater fault than to speak many words that do not belong to the question — yet whoever considers the speech thoroughly will find nothing in it superfluous, for the accusation was of apostasy, and the whole narration maintains that he holds the God the fathers always worshipped. Henry looks at the speaker rather than the speech: he appears ready and mighty in the Scriptures, able to relate the stories pertinent to his purpose without looking in his Bible.

Two further observations belong to nobody else. Robertson defends the report as genuine against the suggestion that it was composed for the occasion: its style is less like the writer's own than the narrative around it, it shows a knowledge of Jewish tradition a Greek would be unlikely to possess, and Saul heard it delivered and Philip almost certainly did, either of whom could have supplied the account. Henry infers from the abrupt ending that the speech we have is not the whole of it, since it breaks off just as it reaches the main point, and would have run much longer had his enemies allowed it — a point Barnes makes as well. Gill contributes only the readings of the versions, which supply the words spoken to him.
2:
Ellicott opens with a critical estimate of the speech that nobody else attempts. It is an unfinished fragment, the torso of a great defence, interrupted by the clamour of the bystanders; and its very incompleteness he takes for indirect proof that the report is true though not verbatim, since a later writer composing a speech in the manner of the Greek historians would have made it a far more direct answer to the indictment — which raises a presumption in favour of the other speeches in the same book. He thinks the report came from Paul, given his prominence among the accusers, and finds it confirmed by parallels with his later teaching; and he calls the speech the first survey of Israel's history as a process of divine education. Wesley supplies the structural key in a sentence: the law is more ancient than the temple, and the promise more ancient than the law.

On the address Clarke corrects the English. The Greek should not be rendered as three classes, since putting a comma after men makes Stephen address elders, scribes and people separately when there were only two; the idiom is the ordinary Greek one which nobody renders men-Athenians or men-Persians. Robertson divides the same two, spectators and members of the court. Calvin asks why Stephen concedes the title at all, and answers that he gives it to the order God appointed, not by flattery, and only as long as that authority stands — then turns it against those who would make the reverence of a place a reason for subscribing to wicked decrees. Barnes and Robertson agree that the God of glory is itself part of the defence, refuting the charge of blasphemy in the opening words, Robertson connecting the glory with the visible radiance of the divine presence.

Whether the call in the third verse is the call of Genesis divides them. Gill denies it: those words were spoken in Haran and these in Mesopotamia, and they are not the same words, nothing being said here of leaving his father's house. Lightfoot gives the reason: Abraham did not leave his father's house when he left Ur, for he took his father and whole family with him, but when he removed from Charran, leaving his father buried behind him. Barnes assumes the Genesis passage and turns to the faith it required, to go almost alone into a land whose situation was unknown. Calvin reads the deferral as the trial: God assigns no land and leaves him in doubt, so that showing it later differs little from having deceived him — and he applies this to men carried into great undertakings by a godly warmth who repent as soon as the heat cools.

The chronology of the fourth verse then produces five separate answers. Lightfoot states it and attacks the Greek translators for appending and he died to every name in the genealogy against the purpose of Moses. Barnes canvasses a textual solution, the Samaritan copy reading a hundred and five where the Hebrew and every other version reads two hundred and five, and a second, that Abraham need not have been born in his father's seventieth year. Ellicott sets out that second solution more fully, Abraham being named first for honour rather than age as Shem is among the sons of Noah, then declines it, judging it more natural that the speaker's memory, or his reporter's, held to the broad outline and was indifferent to the detail. Robertson reports the same solution from two commentators and says plainly that no explanation seems certain. Wesley harmonises instead: while Terah lived Abraham lived partly with him and partly in Canaan, and only after his death altogether in Canaan. Calvin leaves the numbers alone and asks why Abraham stopped at Charran, preferring his father's sickness, since the speech says expressly that he was brought thence after his father died.
5:
That Abraham owned nothing in the land is agreed, and the reason is the same in four hands: the field he held was bought, and what is bought is not given. Barnes adds that it was a burial place and never a residence, Clarke that Jacob's parcel was bought too, Wesley that the purchase itself showed he was a stranger. Calvin draws three things from it: that God exercised his servant's patience, that a possession serving none of the uses of this life is no possession, and that where the thing was wanting the promise was the stay. Robertson notes the proverbial phrase for a foot's tread and the grammar emphasising that there was as yet no child at all, so that Abraham held nothing but the promise of the land and the heir. Lightfoot turns the observation into a weapon: if the patriarchs had no burying place but what they paid for, the persecutors listening had no ground to persuade themselves, on a promise made to their fathers, that the land would be theirs for ever however they behaved.

The four hundred years bring out four ways of handling a discrepancy. Clarke settles it in a line: Moses, Paul and Josephus all say four hundred and thirty, and Stephen uses the round number, dropping the odd tens, as everyone does who is not writing professedly on chronology. Barnes sets the figures side by side and calls the passage one of great perplexity. Ellicott goes behind it: he observes that Paul appears to follow the Greek version, which inserts in the land of Canaan and is supported by the Samaritan copy, and concludes that precision of this kind is not to be looked for here. Robertson adds that no single solution commends itself. Chrysostom does not count at all but presses the interval: if freedom was not to come for four hundred years, no wonder a promised kingdom is long delayed, and the lapse of time did not falsify the word.

At the seventh verse two notice the closing phrase has been moved. Robertson says it is quoted from the sign given to Moses, where it refers to Horeb, and that Stephen applies it to the promised land. Ellicott says the same and accounts for it by the freedom natural to a narrative given from memory, the speaker having substituted they shall serve me for the simpler words of Genesis. On the verb rendered judge Clarke distinguishes the three things a judge does and settles on punishment, which is Barnes's reading too; Calvin ties the judgement to the deliverance, God punishing the oppressor for his people's sake.

The covenant of circumcision is where the defence turns, and three traditions make the same argument. Calvin observes that by confessing circumcision to be God's covenant Stephen clears himself of the charge, while showing that the Jews are wrong to place the beginning of salvation in the outward sign, since Abraham was called and the land promised before he was circumcised. Gill notes that the phrase is the Jews' own, their liturgy carrying a collect for the covenant of circumcision. Chrysostom puts it as an exclamation, that through all those years of promise there was nowhere sacrifice and nowhere circumcision. Ellicott concedes what the others do not: Stephen does not deny having said that Jesus would change the customs, and probably had taught that the change was coming; what he asserts is that the covenant of circumcision followed the promise and so was not the ground of the election, and that being part of a provisional system it is still of God's appointment and to be spoken of with reverence. Calvin adds from the sixth verse the point the speech is built on, that the Church of God was kept elsewhere than in that land, and the fathers preserved before ever the temple stood or the ceremonies were given.
9:
Two numbers in this passage disagree with the Hebrew text, and between them they draw more comment than anything else in the speech. On the seventy-five souls, five agree on the source and differ on what follows from it. Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley all trace the figure to the Greek version, which at the corresponding place adds descendants of Joseph to the sixty-six — Clarke naming the five persons it inserts, Wesley counting a son and a grandson of Manasseh with three children of Ephraim. Ellicott adds that the insertion was probably an editorial correction made from the census in Numbers, and then says outright what the others leave alone: Stephen, being a Hellenistic Jew, accepted without troubling to investigate the number he found in his Greek Bible. Calvin will not leave it there. He reports the older suggestion that the reporter did not set the words down exactly, or took the number from the Greek because he had no Hebrew, and then raises a possibility nobody else raises — that the Greek translators may not have written the number deliberately at all, but that it crept in afterwards by negligence, which is the more credible because the Greeks wrote their numbers in letters. Lightfoot goes further still and questions the unity of the version itself: the same books give a different figure elsewhere, and he can account for it only by supposing that the translator of one book was not the translator of the others.

The burial at Sychem is harder, because two purchases and two graves have to be got out of one sentence, and here there are five distinct answers. Wesley makes it a compression: the speaker, running rapidly over many circumstances, contracts two sepulchres, two places and two purchases into one, naming the buyer in the first case and omitting the seller, naming the seller in the second and omitting the buyer — a concise manner of speaking, he says, common among the Hebrews where the story was notorious. Ellicott looks for a tradition rather than a figure of speech. The words appear to include Jacob, who was buried at Machpelah; limiting them to the patriarchs is tenable but leaves the Old Testament silent about every burial but Joseph's; Josephus places the twelve at Hebron, which is at best a local tradition, while by Jerome's day their tombs were shown at Shechem, and that Samaritan tradition, which survives still, may be the one the speaker followed. Clarke quotes a bishop who declines to choose: since the Old Testament says nothing, the authority of this passage for Sychem is at least as good as that of Josephus for Hebron. Calvin canvasses the answers, notes that the same writer reports seeing the sepulchres of the twelve in one place and only Joseph's grave in another, suggests that empty tombs may have been raised to the rest, and concludes that he can affirm nothing for certain. Robertson takes the boldest line: he reports a commentator who is sure the text as we have it is wrong, observes that the critical text of the New Testament is held to contain some sixty primitive errors, and allows that this may be another — for if the name of Jacob were read in place of Abraham the whole matter would clear up.

The smaller notes belong to the same difficulty. Gill records that one version reads the verb in the singular, as though it were said of Jacob alone, and objects that Jacob is not in question here at all, only the patriarchs. Barnes remarks that the Old Testament mentions the carrying of no bones but Joseph's, while holding the thing probable in itself, since those who carried his would naturally have taken the others.
17:
Henry makes the arithmetic itself the lesson: through the first half of the interval since the promise the covenant family grew only to seventy, and in the second half to six hundred thousand fighting men — the motion of providence being quickest, he says, as it comes nearest the centre, so that nobody should be discouraged by the slowness of the earlier stages. Calvin fastens on the timing of the birth. Moses was born at the very moment when the king had ordered the male children destroyed, so that the minister of deliverance seems dead before he is born; and that is the fittest time for God to work, when nothing is to be hoped or contrived from men.

The phrase describing the child divides four ways over two words. Barnes takes it as a Hebraism, the name of God attached to anything lofty or splendid, as in the mountains of God and the cedars of God, so that it means no more than that the boy was very handsome — and he infers that his mother preserved him on account of his beauty. Clarke calls it divinely beautiful. Ellicott agrees on the idiom, the highest excellence being conceived as what approves itself as good to God; and he notes that a Jewish historian describes the infant's beauty as making passers-by turn to gaze. Robertson breaks with all three. He construes the dative as fair as God looked at him, and derives the adjective from the word for a city, so that it carries the sense of urbanity rather than of beauty at all. On the taking up he adds that the verb was the ordinary one for picking up an exposed infant, and that adoption is meant. Wesley draws the providence out of the exposure: by being cast out Moses came to be bred for a kingdom and given an education he could not otherwise have had.

What the wisdom of the Egyptians amounted to is described by five, doubted by one. Gill and Clarke both give the list from a Jewish philosopher — arithmetic, geometry, music, medicine, hieroglyphics, Chaldean astronomy — and then part company: Gill adds expressly that Moses was no magician and skilled in no unlawful arts, while Clarke reports that the rabbis apply the word wisdom here to magic, and cites a Jewish book claiming nine of the world's ten portions of wisdom for Egypt. Barnes confines the learning to astrology, dream interpretation, medicine, mathematics and the sacred science hidden in the hieroglyphics, and observes that science passed from Egypt to Phoenicia and thence to Greece. Robertson credits the priestly caste with the sciences and calls Moses, like Paul, a man of the schools. Ellicott alone asks where the statement comes from, and answers that the Pentateuch nowhere makes it: it is implied by the adoption and agrees with later expansions of the history, whose currency is shown by the naming of the Egyptian magicians and the dispute over the body of Moses elsewhere in the New Testament. He then finds a purpose in it, an indirect plea for the recognition of secular learning of the kind two later apologists would make.

On the closing words Clarke takes them to cover both the doctrines Moses taught and the deeds ascribed to him, including a campaign against the Ethiopians. Robertson notes the identical phrase is used of Christ in the Gospel. Wesley distinguishes kinds of power in speech: deep, solid and weighty, though not of ready utterance. Calvin will not let the education pass without its danger, a man puffed up with profane sciences having every chance of despising the common people; and he presses the questions carnal reason raises — why God should wink so long at the people's misery, why let Pharaoh rage, and why suffer the deliverer to be cut off from his own kindred and bred in the king's house.
23:
The forty years are not in Scripture and all four who notice it say so. Gill states flatly that the record is silent about the age and the figure comes from tradition; Barnes calls it a constant tradition and quotes the threefold division, forty years in the palace, forty in Midian, forty ministering to Israel; Clarke gives the same saying. Lightfoot alone shows what kind of thing the tradition is. The same threefold forty is told of two rabbis besides, one who traded forty years and studied forty and ministered forty, another illiterate forty years then studying forty and ministering forty — so the pattern is a received schema, not a chronology peculiar to Moses. Robertson takes the phrase about the heart for a Hebrew image, the purpose coming up as if from the lower deeps of the man.

Whether Moses had always known his own people is the first real division, and Clarke and Calvin take opposite sides. Clarke holds the desire was infused into him early by the Spirit of God, and finds its effect in his refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, renouncing a right to the Egyptian crown. Calvin reports that many gather from the verse that Moses was never estranged in mind from his nation, and judges that the words incline the other way — that the Spirit awoke his mind at length, as out of sleep, so that he went at last to visit brethren he had long neglected; he thinks Moses cannot have been ignorant of his stock, bearing a token of it in his flesh, but that it was long before he had courage to own it. Wesley says only that the impulse was probably from God.

The sharpest point in the passage is a conjunction. Ellicott objects that the Greek word never means for, and that rendering it so gives the killing of the Egyptian a deliberate character which the narrative in Exodus does not give it; read as and he supposed, the supposition follows the act instead of explaining it. Robertson construes it the same way, the supposing being added to explain what Moses was thinking when he struck. On what could have grounded such a supposition the answers differ in confidence. Barnes says it is not mentioned by Moses but is not improbable, a man seen taking vengeance on an oppressor being presumed to think himself divinely sent. Clarke supposes Moses expected his commission to be signified to them as it had been to him. Gill grounds it on the public facts, a Hebrew in high life, a wonderful birth, a preservation in infancy and a promise. Lightfoot goes furthest: Moses had a spirit of prophecy while still in the court, and knew himself designed to redeem Israel — and though Moses says nothing of this, the speaker relates it on good authority and with the consent of his countrymen.

On the failure of the attempt the notes converge. Robertson remarks on the rhetorical force of the bare statement that they did not understand, and Wesley puts their stupidity and sloth down as the reason Moses was afterwards unwilling to go to them. Ellicott corrects two smaller things in the next verse: the better copies read was bringing them to peace rather than the completed act, and the address is not a form of politeness but the bare statement ye are brethren. Robertson calls the imperfect conative, so Moses only tried to reconcile them. Calvin takes the incident as the turn of the whole argument: the fault belongs not to the one man who spoke but to all of them, since had they been thankful they would with one consent have checked his insolence, whereas they kept silence and let the benefit be thrown back at their deliverer.
30:
Henry makes the whole passage a reply to the indictment: let anyone judge whether these are the words of a man who blasphemed Moses, since nothing could be spoken more honourably of him. He also reads the delay as design: forty years buried alive in Midian, and only at eighty entering on his office, so that everything afterwards should appear the product of divine power, as Isaac was shown a child of promise by being born to parents past age. Gill reckons the same eighty years from the two forties, and Calvin turns to what they cost: it was a hard exchange to be thrust from a sumptuous life into the base office of feeding sheep, and no man of sense could have avoided the doubts such an interval breeds.

Two names for the mountain and two names for the bush are settled without much dispute. Barnes says the difference between Sinai and Horeb is no contradiction, the two being peaks of one pile springing from a common base; Robertson calls them probably peaks of one range and gives the sense of each name; Ellicott notes only that the less familiar name has been replaced by the more familiar. On the shrub Ellicott identifies the Hebrew word with a thorny acacia still growing there and the Greek with the bramble or any prickly bush, and Robertson agrees. Clarke passes the whole passage over, referring it to his notes on the Exodus narrative.

Who appeared in the bush is a real division. Robertson takes the angel of the one verse to be Jehovah himself in the next, and identifies him with the Angel of the Presence, the eternal Word; Wesley says the same in a line, the angel being the Son of God, as appears from his styling himself Jehovah. Ellicott declines the question as not belonging to the interpretation and then offers a rule that reverses their arrangement: nearly all divine manifestations in the Old Testament addressed to sight resolve into appearances of angels, while those addressed to hearing alone are revelations by the Son as the Word — so that on his account it is the voice and not the figure in the flame that is the Word. Calvin is interested in something else: God dealt with the fathers so that they might know his majesty for certain, a manifest distinction being drawn between his visions and the counterfeits of Satan; otherwise what credit could the oracles carry in which the covenant of eternal life is contained.

The words spoken from the bush are then put to a use they do not have in Exodus, and three do it in two directions. Robertson recalls that Christ used them against the Sadducees to prove the resurrection, since God describes himself as the God of the living. Ellicott presses this into the trial itself: the speaker probably knew the saying had been so used, and the priestly members of the council, being Sadducees, could not have forgotten it — words once urged on them as a proof of immortality now returning attached to the claim that the one who used them has himself been raised. Cyril turns the same verse against a different opponent, the Samaritans, who receive the Law and reject the prophets, so that any argument for the life to come must be made from the Law alone; and this text, he says, must mean the God of those who have being and subsistence. Calvin explains why God takes such a title at all: his majesty is infinite, and our senses are swallowed up if we try to reach it, so he clothes himself in names under which he can be apprehended. Gill and Barnes add that the covenant with the fathers is what the title recalls, and the promise to bring their posterity out.
35:
Four of them see the same thing in the repeated demonstrative, and one of them hears it as a charge. Robertson counts the anaphora, this Moses, this same, five times over, and says the parallel drawn is between Moses and Jesus, those in Egypt having denied the one as these hearers denied the other. Barnes finds the purpose to be preparation: the refusal is dwelt on to show this had always been the nation's character, laying ground for the charge of stiffneckedness that follows. Ellicott locates the parallel in a single word, the noun for deliverer occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and formed from the word for a ransom, chosen to press the likeness. Chrysostom drives it hardest: the man in danger of his life, the man set at naught, the man they declined — this same God raised up and sent; and their who made thee a ruler he sets beside the we have no king but Caesar of the hearers' own generation.

Wesley answers the objection the others pass over. It was not these men who refused Moses but their fathers, forty years before; and God imputes the sin of the fathers to the children who are of the same spirit. He also settles the identification of the angel by a name: the one who spoke on the mount called himself Jehovah, which no created angel could assume without the highest presumption. Calvin takes the refusal as proof that the deliverance was not earned: when the appointed deliverer stood ready they stopped his way, so that God delivered them, as he puts it, against their will; and the miracles that follow display that grace and authenticate the calling.

At the promise of a prophet the drift becomes explicit and several say so. Clarke states it bluntly, that the Moses they honour announced the very prophet they lately put to death. Robertson calls it a neat turn, since the argument makes the men opposing Jesus the real opponents of Moses. Ellicott notes that the parallelism, till now only suggested, is here proclaimed, and adds an observation about the rest of the speech: at this point the council may be supposed to have caught the drift and begun to stir, the effect of which is perhaps traceable in the greater compression of what follows. Calvin holds that the words prove Christ the end of the law though the speaker does not say so in terms, and adds the caution that the prophecy, applied to Christ, agrees to the other prophets as well.

Two questions attach to the last verse. On the assembly in the wilderness Ellicott traces the English word — the earlier versions gave congregation and assembly, the translators of 1611 church by their standing instructions — and defends the choice, since it carries the thought that the society of believers answers in character to the older body; Robertson says congregation is the better rendering. Gill takes the phrase for encouragement, that God always has a church though it be sometimes in a wilderness, and reckons it a greater honour to Moses to have stood in it than to have stood in Pharaoh's court. On the law given by angels, Clarke makes Moses only a mediator between the angel and the people; Barnes agrees the law is so represented while insisting the giver was God himself, so that by the angel the speaker designates him who was God; Robertson objects that the Exodus narrative mentions no angel at all, and contrasts Moses as middle man with the Mediator of a better covenant. Clarke and Wesley agree on the oracles being called living, Clarke because they promise life at three levels, Wesley because the word applied by the Spirit is itself living and powerful.
39:
Robertson says openly what the narrative has been building toward: the story has been patiently led this far so that the home-thrust may be made. Ellicott notes that the word for thrusting Moses away is the one used of the man who thrust him away earlier, so the nation repeats its own act; Calvin finds the horror in the direction of the longing, since to desire the customs of Egypt where they had lately suffered such things is more than blind fury, and adds that they turned back in mind and not in body. Ellicott then makes a point about the calf nobody else makes. The plural gods follows the Greek version, but the Hebrew behind it is plural in form and singular in sense, so the sin broke the second commandment and not the first — an image of the true God, not another god.

That God abandoned them to the consequence is stated by three in the same terms. Henry makes it the punishment of the earlier sin and the pattern of a later one, God saying in effect, let them alone, as he afterwards gave the heathen up to a reprobate mind. Robertson supplies the verbal link, the same verb standing three times in the Pauline passage about the heathen, falling, he says, like clods on a coffin. Calvin describes the mechanism: the first fall was the entrance to a labyrinth, and it was just vengeance that their madness grew until one idol became many — from which he draws the rule that a small departure from what God prescribes carries a man among endless superstitions.

The quotation from the prophet raises an awkward question, since the Pentateuch plainly records sacrifices in the wilderness. Ellicott states the inconsistency and lets the emphasis of the question carry the sense; Clarke answers it by quality rather than fact, granting that sacrifices were offered but denying that they were offered with an upright heart, so that they were too imperfect to be owned; Wesley says the same more briefly, that they had offered many and God accepted none. Lightfoot shows the difficulty was already old: the rabbis had disputed whether the daily sacrifice was offered at Sinai at all, one holding that rules were given but the sacrifice not offered, another that it was offered and never ceased — and a later commentator cited this very verse to settle it. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all note that the twelve minor prophets counted as one book, whence the citation from the book of the prophets.

The two names in the last verse defeat them. Clarke sets the Greek and the Hebrew side by side — the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of Remphan against the tabernacle of your Molech and Chiun your images — and concludes that the place is obscure and the two texts do not cast light on each other. Ellicott inclines to the proper name, so that the phrase is Siccuth your king, while allowing that the prohibition of Moloch worship in the law favours the common rendering. Robertson gives the god as an ox-headed image hollow underneath for fire and the star as a Coptic name for Saturn, and adds that some take the Hebrew word for statues rather than a name. Wesley identifies the one with Mars in human shape and the other with Saturn under a star. Barnes explains the tabernacle as the portable case or shrine in which such an image was carried, like the silver shrines of Ephesus. Gill traces the god to the Ammonites and identifies him with the calf. Wesley alone notices that the threatened exile has been altered, the prophet having written beyond Damascus where the speech has beyond Babylon, and refers the fulfilment to the Assyrian king.
44:
What the tabernacle was called and why is agreed among five. Barnes takes the witness to be the visible evidence of God's presence, the name attaching indifferently to the tent, the tables or the ark; Wesley confines it to the tables, which is why the ark that held them bears the same title; Ellicott adds that the Greek version uses this phrase where the English elsewhere has the tabernacle of the congregation; Gill gives both Hebrew names and both reasons, that the people assembled there and that the law was laid up in it. Robertson makes a rhetorical observation, that the phrase was probably suggested by the tabernacle of Moloch a few lines before, and that the argument now turns from the people's conduct to the second thing the speech drives at, that God is not tied to one place of worship.

How that argument bears on the indictment is stated most exactly by Ellicott, and the answer he finds is a concession followed by a limit: the speaker admits and asserts the divine sanction given to both tabernacle and temple, and denies only that the sanction makes them final. He puts it again at the mention of David: the speaker acknowledges without reserve that the temple was planned by the man after God's own heart and built by the wisest of men, while the question remains whether it therefore represents a final worship or bears witness rather to its own incompleteness. Clarke reads the design the same way, that the Jews leaned too heavily on outward privileges and had not used the law, the tabernacle or the temple service for the purpose of their institution. Calvin turns it about, to clear God of blame: since he prescribed how he would be worshipped, the errors came of their refusing that form, their two faults being that they were not content with the one rule and that they lost sight of the end the ceremonies were appointed for.

One name divides three of them. Barnes says the Greek should have been rendered Joshua, and Clarke that it ought always to be so rendered in such places to avoid ambiguity and confusion. Ellicott agrees it would generally have been better to give the Hebrew form, then argues that something is gained here by letting the identity of the two names show — and adds an observation belonging to the whole speech, that though the speaker stood on trial as a disciple of Jesus of Nazareth, the name does not pass his lips in the defence except in this mention of the captain of Israel. Robertson notes that the participle for receiving in turn occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and reports the argument from a papyrus that the related noun means a deputy rather than a successor.

At the last two verses the note is that the wish and the work belonged to different men. Barnes and Clarke both explain the refusal by the wars and the blood, Clarke adding that David laid the plan and made provision while Solomon executed it, and Gill saying the same of the son who enjoyed peace. Robertson observes that what David asked for was not a tent but a house, the word being from the same root but meaning a more permanent abode. Wesley remarks that David did not obtain his petition, God remaining without a temple until Solomon built one, and that the word is chosen with an eye to what follows. Calvin meets the suspicion that the speech is glancing at Solomon: what is denied is not Solomon's understanding, who knew well that God is to be sought in heaven and the mind lifted there by faith, and the work itself was undertaken by God's own commandment and with a promise annexed.
48:
Four of them observe that the point is Solomon's own. Clarke refers it directly to the dedication prayer and says both mean that the divine majesty could not be contained in the whole compass of nature, much less in a house built by hands; Wesley says the same in a line; Gill recalls Solomon's wonder that God should dwell on earth when the heaven of heavens could not contain him; Robertson agrees the builder himself foresaw and acknowledged it, and adds a textual note, that the true text has no word for house or temple at all but reads simply in things made with hands.

Why the remark is made here at all is a question Barnes raises and cannot settle: he says frankly that the reason is not very clear, since the speaker had just shown his veneration for the temple by tracing it to God's command — and then supplies what the addition achieves, that if God does not need such a house the house might be destroyed, a new truth being about to be published that his worship is confined to no age or people or nation. Ellicott makes the same point with more weight, that the words broke down any notion of an exclusive holiness in the temple and so placed its fall among the ordinary chastisements God might use; and he alone offers an explanation of where the speaker got such a doctrine, tracing it to a probable connection, direct or indirect, with the Samaritans, whose position on the temple this would echo. Robertson draws out the consequence: the argument proves God a spirit who may be worshipped anywhere by anyone of any race, which he calls a tremendous argument for the universality of Christianity, and whose very strength, he says, angered the court to desperation.

Calvin works on what the quoted words can and cannot mean. The sitting is not to be understood as though God had a body or could be divided into parts after the manner of men; the point is that being infinite he cannot be comprehended within any bounds of place, and that men are deceived who measure God, or the worship due to him, by their own nature. He adds that the prophet was dealing with hypocrites, and so teaches generally that God is unlike men and is not moved by the pomp of this world; and at the last verse he draws the conclusion, that God needs neither gold nor furniture nor sacrifices, wants none of what we offer for his own sake but only to exercise us in godliness, so that his true worship is not contained in ceremonies at all.

Two smaller notes close the passage. Gill observes that the prophet's words are read in the original without the interrogation they carry here, so that what stands as a question in the speech stands there as a plain assertion that God's own hand made all these things. Clarke reconstructs what happened next: the discourse was certainly not finished and the inferences from the facts not yet drawn, but the hearers, perceiving what conclusions were coming against the temple and its ritual, raised a clamour, and that clamour is what turned the defence into the address that follows.
51:
Whether the change of tone is caused by an interruption is the question here, and four say yes while one refuses. Barnes finds the verse has no immediate connexion with what precedes and reads the whole discourse as plainly broken into, conjecturing that the court saw the drift, raised a clamour, and was addressed in these words when the tumult had somewhat subsided. Ellicott says the sudden passage from calm argument to vehement indignation cannot be thought spontaneous, and that loud clamours had by now taken the place of whispered murmurs. Henry reconstructs what was cut off — the speaker was going on to show that the temple service, like the temple, must give way to a worship in spirit and truth — and observes that they could hear the history of their own nation patiently enough, being learned in it, and could not bear the application. Calvin agrees he would have said more, notes that the long approach was used of set purpose to tame hearers who were like brute beasts, and thinks their madness took fire at the point where he proved the law corrupted and the temple polluted. Robertson alone declines the inference: critics assume an interruption because of the sharp tone, and that may be true, but the natural climax of the argument is explanation enough.

The two epithets are traced by everyone to the older Scriptures, and two make more of them. Clarke takes the first from oxen that cannot be broken to the yoke, whose necks will not bend either way, and expounds the second at length from the meaning of circumcision as a type of purity. Robertson notes that both compounds occur in the Greek Old Testament and nowhere else in the New. Ellicott sharpens the second into a reproach: the phrase about the uncircumcised heart had been used by a prophet of strangers, and is here turned upon men who boasted of their exclusive privilege as Israelites. Wesley reads both as predictions rather than descriptions, the uncircumcised heart being shown in what they do three verses later and the uncircumcised ears in what they do six. Lightfoot supplies the most striking parallel in the chapter: a rabbinic story in which, when the people pressed Aaron for gods to go before them, one man resisted and rebuked them as short-necked, asking whether they did not remember what God had done for them — whereupon they rose up and killed him.

On the charge that they resist the Spirit as their fathers did, Gill takes the stiff neck for a refusal of the yoke of God's law, and Wesley makes the resistance perpetual, as often as ever they are called. Cyril, writing of this same scene, puts the matter from the other side: the Spirit wrought not in the apostles only but in the seven, and those who disputed with this man were not able to resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.

At the next verse the sweep of the accusation is measured. Barnes calls the question a strong way of saying they had persecuted all the prophets, and adds that this is not to be taken as literally universal but as the national character. Clarke supplies an instance from tradition, the prophet sawn asunder at a king's command, and then gives the title of the Just One two grounds, the unspotted integrity of the life and the plenary acquittal at Pilate's tribunal. Ellicott says the title does not appear to have been among the received names of the expected Messiah, though it may have been suggested by a prophecy, and that the church at Jerusalem seems to have adopted it; he adds that the reproach echoes words of Christ's own about the treatment of the prophets.
54:
The verb for what the words did to them is rendered by three in the same violent way. Clarke and Ellicott both give it as sawn through, Ellicott adding that this is a keener pang than the pricking that produced repentance at the earlier sermon, and produces frenzy instead; Robertson says the speaker had sent a saw through his hearers that rasped them to the bone. On the gnashing Ellicott notes what nobody else does, that this is the one literal use of a phrase familiar everywhere else as a figure, expressing brute passion and not despair, the court having passed out of articulate speech into animal noise; Robertson compares a pack of snarling wolves and says the man knew what it meant. Calvin traces the progress — the proceeding had some colour of judgment at first, then they interrupted with murmuring, then broke into cries so that not one word more should be heard — and calls it madness rather than anger. Henry sets the whole scene as a contrast of hell in its fire with heaven in its brightness, each serving to set off the other, and observes that no vote is recorded, no verdict and no sentence. Chrysostom turns it on the accusers: the man who had done no wrong and was used like a criminal had the better right to be incensed, yet used no calumny but proved what he said, and the calumniators had the worst of it in the end.

Whether anything happened outwardly at the vision divides two from the plain sense. Calvin denies the heavens were altered at all: nothing was changed in their nature, but a new quickness of sight was granted that pierced every obstacle, since even a rent would leave no human eye able to reach so far — and the sight was given to this man alone. Ellicott says the same, that the vision was for the inward eye and not for sense, and draws the consequence, that no priest or scribe saw anything, so the claim seemed to them a fresh aggravation of guilt. He also explains how the fact could be reported at all, partly from the rapt look of the martyr's face and partly from the words that followed; and the fullness of the Spirit described is a settled state, not a sudden inspiration. Gill and Barnes read the upward look as recourse: seeing no safety in the council, he turned his eyes where protection was to be had. Calvin puts it more starkly, that being destitute of every human help and with nothing but death before his eyes, he turned from the world to the Judge of life and death.

The posture is the last difficulty, and four handle it differently. Robertson observes that everywhere else the Son is pictured seated, and takes the standing for a rising to cheer the man about to die; Wesley reads it as a readiness to receive him; Clarke explains it of his official character as Mediator. Cyril, expounding the same clause, does the opposite and heaps up the testimonies for sitting, from the Gospel, from Peter and from Paul. On the title Ellicott notes that this is the only certain use outside the Gospels of the name the Lord constantly used of himself, and that the speech was delivered years before any Gospel was written. Lightfoot shows where the words come from and what a Jew made of them: the phrase is taken from the vision of Daniel, and a rabbinic commentator on that place says of the one like a son of man that this is the Messiah our righteousness. Barnes calls the opened heaven a figure for being permitted to see within, and Gill compares the opening at the baptism of Christ.
57:
Who did the killing is settled the same way by two. Gill says these were not the council but the common people, and Barnes agrees that he was put to death in a popular tumult. On the stopping of the ears Robertson says they held them shut with their hands and affected to believe the man a blasphemer; Clarke turns the gesture into an argument against them: if Jesus was indeed at God's right hand they had murdered an innocent person and must expect justice to avenge him quickly, which is why they would not let the words be heard. Calvin offers two explanations and chooses: either a vain show of zeal, hypocrites being always pricked into immoderate heat, as with the high priest who rent his clothes at a like saying, or else the preaching of Christ's glory was such a torment that they had to burst out in madness — and he is rather of the second mind, since what follows describes men unable to hold themselves in.

How far this was an execution and how far a lynching produces five answers. Wesley says flatly that they rushed on him before any sentence passed. Clarke says they would not wait for a sentence at all, being determined to stone first and prove afterwards that it had been done justly. Robertson notes that no vote was taken and no scruple raised about the right to put a man to death, and suggests a political occasion, that it fell between the recall of one Roman governor and the arrival of the next, or that the governor connived. Ellicott makes the same point by contrast: at the trial of Christ the forms were observed because the procurator was then in the city, whereas now every restraint was removed — and he observes that neither office nor age has always been protection against such outrage even in Christian assemblies, instancing a notorious synod of the fifth century and the caution that a bishop must not be a striker. Barnes takes the middle position, that though the man was condemned without the regular process some of the forms of law were still observed and he was stoned in the manner the law directed for blasphemers.

Lightfoot supplies the rule that makes Barnes's point good. The place of stoning lay outside the court, on the command to bring the blasphemer without the camp; and the tradition put it outside three camps, the court reckoned the camp of the divine presence, the temple mount the camp of the Levites, the city the camp of Israel — so that in every town the stoning was done beyond the walls. Barnes reports the same custom, that it was not usual to stone in the presence of the council. Ellicott adds the requirement that governed the witnesses: the law made them cast the first stones, so as to impress on them the weight of what their testimony had done, and the flowing outer cloak had to be put off before their arms were free.

Calvin measures the sentence against the statute it invoked. Stoning was appointed for a false prophet, but the same law defines who is one, the man who tries to draw the people to strange gods; so the death was unjust as well as wicked, and the martyrs of Christ suffer the punishment of the wicked, the cause alone making the difference — a difference so esteemed with God that their reproaches outweigh all the glory of the world. Wesley turns from the scene to the young man at whose feet the clothes were laid, and asks whether he could have believed, had anyone told him, that he would one day be stoned in the same cause.
59:
Four commentators from four traditions make the same argument here, and they make it out of a word that is not in the text. Barnes states the fact: the word rendered God stands in none of the ancient copies or versions and should never have been put into the translation, so the sentence says they stoned him while he was invoking and saying, Lord Jesus. Clarke agrees, adding that no early father has it but one, and draws the conclusion — here is a manifest proof that prayer is offered to Christ, in the most solemn circumstance in which prayer can be offered; could a man commit his soul into those hands without conceiving him to be God? Wesley reasons identically, that so solemn a committing of a departing soul is worship no good man could pay to a creature, and that the disciple worships the Son in the very manner in which the Son on the cross worshipped the Father. Ellicott adds the historical witness, that this is direct prayer offered, in a Roman governor's phrase for what he had learned of Christian worship, to Christ as God — and marks the echo, the Son commending his spirit to the Father and the disciple commending his to the Son. Robertson notes that the stoning went on through the prayer, and that many have followed this man into death with the same words on their lips.

Calvin turns to the witnesses who threw first, and finds in the requirement a piece of moral shrewdness: many who will cut an innocent throat by perjury of the tongue are held back when the murder must be done with their own hands, which is why the law laid the first stone on them — and that these men did not flinch shows how blind their ungodliness was, being willing to redden with their hands what they had killed with their tongues. He notes that even in the tumult some show of judgment was kept up.

On the kneeling, Barnes takes it as voluntary, the man choosing the attitude he would die in; Robertson observes that the Greek phrase for it is not the old idiom but one the writer uses five times, and that the kneeling was worship offered to the figure seen standing. The prayer that follows draws the comparison every commentator makes and one presses further. Barnes says it strikingly resembles the dying prayer of Christ and that nothing but the Christian religion would let a man utter it at such a moment; Clarke says the disciple copies his Master in the same spirit and meaning, varying only the expression; Robertson calls it the very spirit of Jesus toward his enemies; Calvin observes that the prayer was made at the instant when cruelty might most have provoked revenge, there being nothing harder than to forgive an injury so. Ellicott goes further and makes the resemblance evidence: it could hardly have been accidental, and shows that the account of the crucifixion was in some measure already known to the speaker. He then names the object he thinks the prayer chiefly had, the foremost of the accusers, and endorses the old saying that the Church owes that man's conversion to this martyr's prayer.

The last phrase is read two ways. Barnes takes falling asleep for the usual scriptural way of describing a saint's death, marking both its peacefulness against the alarm of sinners and the hope of a waking. Lightfoot notes that nothing is more common than the same expression in the rabbinic writers, which sets the usage in a wider frame than the Christian one. Gill observes only that the man seems to have been standing while he commended his soul and knelt for the second prayer, prayer being lawful in either posture.
